meta.title: Who really said "To anger a conservative, lie to him. To anger a liberal, tell him the truth"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No, Theodore Roosevelt never said it. Fact-checkers and the TR Center find no source; the line first surfaced online around 2007, decades after his death.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'To anger a conservative, lie to him. To anger a liberal, tell him the truth'?
meta.ogDescription: A 21st-century internet fabrication falsely pinned on Theodore Roosevelt. No source exists in his speeches or writings; it first appeared in print around 2007.

answer.label: Not Theodore Roosevelt — a modern internet fabrication
answer.authorDates: 1858–1919 · 26th U.S. President; the quote is falsely attributed to him
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Theodore Roosevelt ever said or wrote this. It appears in none of his speeches, letters, or writings, and the Theodore Roosevelt Center found no trace of it ↗. Etymologist Barry Popik dates the full line to print only around 2007 — nearly a century after TR’s death — and it was first attached to Roosevelt around 2009. Its true author is unknown.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from
source.excerpt: To anger a conservative, lie to him. To anger a liberal, tell him the truth.
trail: Etymologist and OED contributor Barry Popik traced the full line to print around 2007 ↗, with only a partial 1995 Usenet variant before it — long after Roosevelt’s death.
FactCheck.org ↗ quotes the Theodore Roosevelt Center and a University of Virginia scholar, both of whom could find no evidence TR said it and doubt its authenticity.
TruthOrFiction ↗ documents the arc: unknown attribution c. 2007, first credited to Roosevelt c. 2009, and regularly linked to him by 2010.
source.excerptNote: No documented source in Roosevelt’s speeches, letters, or writings exists for this wording. A partial precursor — “it’s easy to annoy a liberal, just tell the truth about them’’ — appears on a Usenet group in 1995, per Barry Popik ↗, but the full two-part line only surfaces around 2007.

source.rightsNote: The wording has no identifiable author or source work: it is an anonymous internet-era coinage first seen in print around 2007. Because no originating work or date can be established, no copyright status can be asserted — and it is certainly not a Roosevelt-era public-domain text.

author.name: Theodore Roosevelt
author.heading: About Theodore Roosevelt
author.metaLine: 1858–1919 · 26th U.S. President · the quote is falsely attributed to him
author.bio: Theodore Roosevelt was the 26th President of the United States (1901–1909), a prolific author, and one of the most heavily quoted figures in American history — which makes him a magnet for invented sayings. This partisan zinger is one of many lines pinned on him with no basis in his actual speeches or writings. As scholars note, the modern political labels “liberal” and “conservative” were not even used this way in his era, where “progressive” was the more common term.

misattribution.heading: How the misattribution spread
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook internet misquote: a punchy partisan line dressed up with the name of a long-dead, widely admired president to lend it borrowed authority.

items.why: The Theodore Roosevelt Center and scholars found no trace of it ↗ in his speeches or writings; the full line only reached print around 2007, decades after his 1919 death.
The same line has circulated under Churchill’s name, another all-purpose magnet for unsourced quips, per FactCheck.org ↗.
Gizmodo ↗ notes the quote has also been attributed to the radio host — a sign it is a free-floating modern coinage, not anyone’s documented words.

misattribution.truthLine: The real author is unknown. The wording is an anonymous internet-era coinage first seen in print around 2007, as documented by Barry Popik’s antedating research ↗ — not Theodore Roosevelt, Churchill, or Limbaugh.

context.heading: Why the attribution doesn’t fit
lead: Beyond the missing source, the quote is anachronistic. In Theodore Roosevelt’s day the pairing of “liberal” against “conservative” as the two poles of American politics was not the common framing — “progressive” was the word of the moment, and Roosevelt himself ran as a Progressive in 1912. The line’s neat left/right symmetry reflects a 21st-century culture-war idiom, not early-1900s usage.

Its documented history bears this out: a partial precursor surfaced on a Usenet newsgroup in 1995, the full two-part version reached print around 2007 credited to an “unknown source,” and Roosevelt’s name was grafted on only around 2009.
context.pull: There is no evidence this quote exists before the 21st century — it likely originated on the Internet.
